analyst: Dyson, Eddington & Davidson (reduction: Greenwich, Davidson & Furner)
data_used: 7 eclipse plates x 7 stars (plate 6 clouded out) vs 7 July comparison plates via a scale plate; RA and Dec
method: normal equations, plate constants solved per plate in each coordinate plus deflection coefficient; RA (weight 1) and Dec (weight 2) combined
location: p. 331 (sec. 39); derivation p. 306 (sec. 21-22: alpha = +0.100 rev = +0.625 arcsec at 50 arcmin, Sun's radius 15.8 arcmin)
quote: The result from declinations is about twice the weight of that from right ascensions, so that the mean result is 1″·98 with a probable error of about ±0″·12.
reference: Dyson F. W., Eddington A. S., Davidson C. 1920, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 220, 291-333
notes: sigma = 0.18 arcsec (p.e./0.6745). Same value already in N7 gamma.csv (E1919-sobral-4inch).

data_used: declinations only
method: as above, declination equations only
quote: From declinations . . . 1″·94 / From right ascensions . . . 2″·06
reference: Dyson F. W., Eddington A. S., Davidson C. 1920, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 220, 291-333
notes: p. 306 gives the coefficients: RA alpha = +0.105 rev, Dec +0.098 rev (at 50 arcmin).

data_used: right ascensions only
method: as above, RA equations only
quote: From right ascensions . . . 2″·06
reference: Dyson F. W., Eddington A. S., Davidson C. 1920, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 220, 291-333
notes: Converting the p. 306 coefficient 0.105 rev x 6.25 arcsec/rev x 50/15.8 gives 2.08 (my arithmetic); the paper prints 2.06.

data_used: 16 eclipse plates (of 19 exposed) vs July comparison plates, declinations only (RA 'of little weight')
method: means of the 16 plates give alpha + 243e = +0.0435 rev; scale e = +0.082 rev from Table IX
quote: or with the value of the scale 0ʳ·082 from the previous table α = + 0ʳ·024 = 0″·93 at the limb.
reference: Dyson F. W., Eddington A. S., Davidson C. 1920, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 220, 291-333
notes: No error published. p. 331: 'discordant by an amount much beyond the limits of its accidental error'.

data_used: same as above
method: same equations but scale change fixed at the value from refraction and aberration (e = +0.020 rev) instead of the fitted +0.082
quote: It may be noticed that the change of scale arising from differences of refraction and aberration is 0ʳ·020. If this value of e be taken instead of 0ʳ·082 we obtain α = + 0ʳ·039 = + 1″·52 at the sun's limb.
reference: Dyson F. W., Eddington A. S., Davidson C. 1920, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 220, 291-333
notes: Kennefick (2007, 2009) stresses that this alternative is close to Harvey's 1979 re-measurement (1.55).

data_used: same as above
method: least squares per plate (alpha and e free for each plate), mean of plates
quote: The mean result for α is 0″·99, or very nearly the same as that already found.
reference: Dyson F. W., Eddington A. S., Davidson C. 1920, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 220, 291-333

data_used: all stars, 18 plate comparisons (16 plates; plates 7 and 12 each measured against two comparison plates)
method: plain mean of the 18 per-plate values in Table IX (d, e, alpha solved per plate; 1r = 12.3 arcsec)
location: Table IX mean row and text, p. 310
quote: Thus the mean value of α obtained from all the astrographic plates is 0″·86, a figure considerably less than that obtained from the 4-inch photographs.
reference: Dyson F. W., Eddington A. S., Davidson C. 1920, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 220, 291-333
notes: Mean row also checked in the parallel transcription dyson1920_table9_astrographic.csv (15.48/18 = 0.860). Quoted by Earman & Glymour (p. 74), Gilmore & Tausch-Pebody (Table A1) and Campbell 1923 (PASP 35, 19).

data_used: 2 plates (W, X) x 5 stars vs Oxford comparison plates; scale from Oxford/Principe check plates (Arcturus field)
method: scale fixed from check plates; iterative solution for orientation; 4 plate comparisons
quote: There is further the error of ±0″·14 affecting all four results equally, arising from the determination of scale. Taking this into account, and including the small correction −0″·04 previously mentioned, our result may be written 1″·61±0″·30.
reference: Dyson F. W., Eddington A. S., Davidson C. 1920, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 220, 291-333
notes: sigma = 0.44. Accidental p.e. alone 0.25 (p. 328).

data_used: plate U (reduced at Principe)
method: as for W, X
quote: This gives the deflection 2″·90. The probable error is, however, ± 0″·87, so that the result is practically worthless. ... This determination is ignored in the subsequent discussion.
reference: Dyson F. W., Eddington A. S., Davidson C. 1920, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 220, 291-333
notes: Gilmore & Tausch-Pebody (note 33) round this to 2.9 +- 0.9.

data_used: astrographic plates
method: scale from the eclipse plates themselves
quote: The astrographic plates gave 0″·97 for the displacement at the limb when the scale-value was determined from the plates themselves, and 1″·40 when the scale-value was assumed from the check-plates. But the much better plates gave for the displacement at the limb 1″·98, Einstein's predicted value being 1·75.
reference: Thomson J. J. (chair) 1919, 'Joint eclipse meeting of the Royal Society and the Royal Astronomical Society', The Observatory 42, 389-398 (ADS 1919Obs....42..389.)
notes: Differs from the 1920 report (0.93 / 1.52). Same passage: 'Mr. Davidson secured 15 out of 18 photographs showing the required stellar images' and 'Dr. Crommelin with the other lens had 7 successful plates out of 8' (p. 390).

data_used: astrographic plates
method: scale 'assumed from the check-plates'
quote: (see row above)
reference: Thomson J. J. (chair) 1919, 'Joint eclipse meeting of the Royal Society and the Royal Astronomical Society', The Observatory 42, 389-398 (ADS 1919Obs....42..389.)

data_used: 2 plates x 5 stars
method: scale from check plates
quote: we obtained as the final result from the two plates for the value of the displacement at the limb 1″·6±0″·3. The p.e. was determined from the residuals of individual stars.
reference: Thomson J. J. (chair) 1919, 'Joint eclipse meeting of the Royal Society and the Royal Astronomical Society', The Observatory 42, 389-398 (ADS 1919Obs....42..389.)

data_used: astrographic plates
method: scale change assumed real
quote: If it is assumed that the scale has changed, then the Einstein deflection from the series of plates is 0.90″; if it is assumed that no real change of focus occurred, but merely a blurring of the images, the result is 1.56″; little weight is, however, attached to this series of photographs. (as quoted by Kennefick 2009, p. 41)
reference: Dyson F. 1921, Nature 106, 786
notes: Quoted identically by Kennefick 2009 and Gilmore & Tausch-Pebody (p. 8). Primary not read.

data_used: astrographic plates
method: no real scale change, only blurring
quote: (see row above)
reference: Dyson F. 1921, Nature 106, 786

data_used: astrographic plates
method: scale from the July plates, bad focus assumed not to alter scale
quote: This instrument [the Astrographic] supports the Newtonian shift ... Making the assumption that the bad focus did not alter the scale, and deducing this [scale], from the July plates, the value of the shift becomes 1.52″. (as quoted by Kennefick 2007, arXiv:0709.0685)
reference: Crommelin A. C. D. 1919, Nature 104, 280
notes: Primary not read.

data_used: DED's published 4-inch star displacements (7 plates x 7 stars), plus second-order refraction terms (Turner's formulae)
method: least squares, six plate constants + deflection (his 'solution 4', equivalent to the Report's reduction)
quote: The deflection at the Sun's limb comes out 2″·00 in solution 4 as against 1″·98 in the Report,—an agreement far within the probable error.
reference: Russell H. N. 1920, 'Note on the Sobral eclipse photographs', MNRAS 81, 154-164 (ADS 1920MNRAS..81..154R)
notes: Table IV: correction to the theoretical 0.553 arcsec at 50 arcmin = +0.080 (sol. 4), +0.118 (x only), +0.061 (y only), +0.101 (sol. 2: four constants, no distortion). Converting sol. 2 to the limb gives ~2.07 (my arithmetic, not printed). Mean error of one coordinate difference 0.263 arcsec, p.e. +-0.177 per pair (p. 157).

data_used: as above
method: linear 'pure strain' term (a-e, b+d) beyond scale and rotation; mean of solutions 3 and 4
quote: whence (taking the mean of solutions 3 and 4) p = 62° ± 7°; S = 0″·26 ± 0″·06 at unit distance (50′).
reference: Russell H. N. 1920, 'Note on the Sobral eclipse photographs', MNRAS 81, 154-164 (ADS 1920MNRAS..81..154R)
notes: p. 160: 'The existence of a distortion of the eclipse field appears to be proved.' Sums of squares of residuals (Table V): theory+no distortion 0.1623 (0.0990 expected), fitted+no distortion 0.1303 (0.0891), theory+distortion 0.0479 (0.0792), fitted+distortion 0.0244 (0.0693). Russell attributes the distortion to the coelostat mirror (p. 161). The +- is a p.e. ('The probable errors are computed from the weights').

data_used: DED's published 4-inch measures
method: re-reduction with emphasis on the scale value
quote: Englische Expedition 1919, 6 m-Kamera, E = 2″,0 bzw. 2″,2.
reference: Freundlich E., v. Klueber H., v. Brunn A. 1931, Z. Astrophys. 3, 171-198 (ADS 1931ZA......3..171F)
notes: Read from the OCR in 64-gravity-scorecard/data/literature/papers/gamma-freundlich1931. pp. 193-194: the 1919 data 'fuer einen Wert der Lichtablenkung sprechen, der noch oberhalb des damals errechneten Wertes E = 2″,0 naeher an 2″,2 liegt'.

data_used: DED's mean displacements of the 7 stars (4-inch only)
method: straight-line fit of displacement against 1/r with a free scale-type parameter q; radial displacements; RA alone 2.11 (q = -0.012), Dec alone 2.00 (q = -0.001)
quote: Les observations de 1919 sont donc compatibles dans la limite des erreurs d'observation avec l'existence d'un déplacement inversement proportionnel à la distance, atteignant 2″,06 au bord du soleil.
reference: Danjon A. 1932, 'Le deplacement apparent des etoiles autour du soleil eclipse', J. Phys. Radium 3, 281-301
notes: Mean of the 7 single-star values 2.05 with 'ecart moyen' 0.20 (p. 289). Danjon got 2.05 (Lick 15-ft), 2.07 (Lick 5-ft) and 2.06 (Potsdam 1929) the same way and adopted 2.06.

data_used: Dyson & Woolley (1937) revised deflections of the 7 stars, corrected for second-order refraction
method: least squares on Delta_r = A/r + B r (one scale term)
quote: I used these deflections for forming the equations of condition (2), which were solved by the method of least-squares, and obtained A = 2″·07 ± 0″·09 p.e. and the scale correction B = − 0″·0158
reference: Mikhailov A. A. 1959, MNRAS 119, 593-608
notes: With A fixed at 1.75: B = +0.0068; sums of squared residuals (0.01 arcsec units) 360 (A free), 690 (A = 1.75), 402 (straight line a + b r). Already in N7 notes.

data_used: star deflections of 9 eclipse data sets incl. 1919 (Mikhailov's scale corrections)
method: per-star scale-corrected deflections binned in distance
reference: Merat P., Pecker J.-C., Vigier J.-P., Yourgrau W. 1974, A&A 32, 471-475 (ADS 1974A&A....32..471M)
notes: Their claim (Table 3): excess over GR of +0.139 +- 0.033 arcsec at a mean distance of 3.43 solar radii, +0.081 +- 0.024 at 6.14, consistent with GR beyond ~5 radii. A fringe interpretation (a 'dispersive medium'); not followed up by later radio results.

analyst: G. M. Harvey (measurements E. D. Clements, software A. Murray), RGO
data_used: the surviving plates re-measured in 1978 on the Zeiss Ascorecord: 5 eclipse + 5 comparison plates (one eclipse plate missing, one broken, one comparison missing)
method: positions per plate; comparison plates combined into one reference catalogue; per plate lambda*(DED predicted 1.75 displacement) + 6 linear plate constants by least squares; weighted mean of plates
location: Table III, p. 198; lambda = 1.09 +- 0.06 in Table II, p. 197
quote: 4-inch plates measured on the Zeiss 1·90 ± 0·11
reference: Harvey G. M. 1979, 'Gravitational deflection of light', The Observatory 99, 195-198 (ADS 1979Obs....99..195H)
notes: Per-plate lambda (Table II): 1.08+-0.16, 1.15+-0.25, 1.11+-0.09, 0.85+-0.21, 1.12+-0.11. Tables are being transcribed by another agent.

data_used: 9 eclipse + 9 comparison astrographic plates (those with the 10 most common images), both coordinates
method: as above
location: Table III, p. 198; lambda = 0.88 +- 0.19 in Table II, p. 197
quote: Where the previous reduction yielded a value of 0″·93 with an unspecified, large error, the new determination is 1″·55±0″·34.
reference: Harvey G. M. 1979, 'Gravitational deflection of light', The Observatory 99, 195-198 (ADS 1979Obs....99..195H)
notes: 1.55 is 0.6 sigma below 1.75 and 2.0 sigma above 0.87 (my arithmetic). One comparison plate with a very high error of unit weight was excluded; the star nearest the Sun was dropped on plates 2, 6 and 11 (p. 197).

data_used: the two values above
method: weighted mean
quote: Combining the two fresh determinations, weighted according to their standard errors, gives 1″·87±0″·13, a result which is just within one standard error of the predicted value.
reference: Harvey G. M. 1979, 'Gravitational deflection of light', The Observatory 99, 195-198 (ADS 1979Obs....99..195H)

data_used: DED's published results; Sobral astrographic per-plate values
method: p.e. x 1.4826 for 4-inch and Principe; for the Sobral astrographic the scatter of the per-plate values (not an error of the mean)
quote: The standard deviations in seconds of arc are approximately: Principe astrographic, 0.444″; Sobral astrographic, 0.48″; Sobral 4-inch, 0.178″.
reference: Earman J., Glymour C. 1980, Hist. Stud. Phys. Sci. 11(1), 49-85
notes: Gilmore & Tausch-Pebody's central criticism: 0.48 is a dispersion of 18 values, not the uncertainty of their mean.

analyst: Gilmore & Tausch-Pebody (fit by I. Webber, MATLAB lsqr)
data_used: DED's published 4-inch differential positions (14 equations per plate)
method: least squares, Dx = ax+by+c+alpha*Ex, Dy = dx+ey+f+alpha*Ey per plate
location: Table A1 (p. 20) and Table A2 (p. 22) of the online version
quote: Least squares—combined ... 1.99
reference: Gilmore G., Tausch-Pebody G. 2022, Notes Rec. R. Soc. 76(1), 155-180 (online 2020)
notes: Error adopted = DED p.e. converted (0.18). Their LS 'dispersion' 0.33 over 7 plates gives 0.13 on the mean (p. 21). Single-plate fits, not one global fit.

data_used: DED's published declination displacements of 5 stars on the 16 plates
method: least squares per plate, mean of plates
quote: We derive a mean of 0.95 arcsec with a dispersion about that mean of 0.90 arcsec.
reference: Gilmore G., Tausch-Pebody G. 2022, Notes Rec. R. Soc. 76(1), 155-180 (online 2020)
notes: They stress 'there is no model-independent way to use this dispersion to derive a standard error on the mean'; Table A3 nevertheless uses 0.95 +- 0.9.

data_used: DED's published Principe differential positions (2 eclipse plates x 2 comparison plates x 5 stars)
method: least squares
quote: Least squares ... 1.61
reference: Gilmore G., Tausch-Pebody G. 2022, Notes Rec. R. Soc. 76(1), 155-180 (online 2020)
notes: LS dispersion 0.46; adopted error is DED's p.e. converted.

method: inverse-variance weighted mean
quote: Sobral 4-inch + Principe astrograph 1.93 ± 0.17 1.06σ 6.2σ
reference: Gilmore G., Tausch-Pebody G. 2022, Notes Rec. R. Soc. 76(1), 155-180 (online 2020)
notes: 'indicative, not robust'.

data_used: adds Sobral astro 0.95+-0.9
method: inverse-variance weighted mean
quote: Sobral 4-inch + Sobral astrograph + Principe astrograph 1.90 ± 0.16 0.94σ 6.4σ
reference: Gilmore G., Tausch-Pebody G. 2022, Notes Rec. R. Soc. 76(1), 155-180 (online 2020)

data_used: as above but Sobral astro error = 0.48 (Earman & Glymour's dispersion)
method: inverse-variance weighted mean
quote: Sobral 4-inch + Sobral astrograph with error = 0.48 arcsec + Principe astrograph 1.82 ± 0.16 0.44σ 5.9σ
reference: Gilmore G., Tausch-Pebody G. 2022, Notes Rec. R. Soc. 76(1), 155-180 (online 2020)
notes: Even granting Earman & Glymour's error, the combination stays 5.9 sigma from the half deflection.

data_used: secondary
method: quoted
quote: corresponding to a deflection at the limb of the Sun (grazing ray) of 1.60 ± 0.31 arcseconds, or 0.91 ± 0.18 times the Einsteinian prediction
reference: Will C. M. 2015, Class. Quantum Grav. 32, 124001 (arXiv:1409.7812)
notes: Not what DED printed (1.61 +- 0.30 p.e.). Do not use.

data_used: 18 passes (DSS 25, ~8 h each; pass dates ~9 June to ~4 July 2002 read from Fig. 3); 1094 points at 300 s; open-loop Radio Science receiver data (per Anderson et al. 2004); X/X, X/Ka, Ka/Ka plasma calibration + troposphere calibration
method: ODP fit in the BCRS ('final 9-parameter fit on the calibrated data')
quote: Our result, γ = 1 + (2.1 ± 2.3) × 10⁻⁵, agrees with the predictions of standard general relativity
reference: Bertotti B., Iess L., Tortora P. 2003, Nature 425, 374-376
notes: 'at 1-sigma': Ashby & Bertotti 2010, CQG 27, 145013, eq. (1). Residual rms 1.2e-4 Hz on the 8.4 GHz carrier at 300 s (= 1.4e-14 fractional, my arithmetic); Allan deviation 0.7e-14 at 1000 s (Bertotti, Ashby & Iess 2008).

data_used: closed-loop Doppler, 1569 points, 17 passes, Tc = 300 s; three-link OL plasma calibration from Iess & Tortora; no water-vapour radiometer calibration
method: ODP; 8 parameters: 6 state + constant radial acceleration + gamma
quote: The solution for the two parameters, exclusive of the six state parameters, is: γ − 1 = (−4.8 ± 5.7) × 10⁻⁵, ar = (−26.7 ± 1.1) × 10⁻⁸ cm/s² where the uncertainties include both random and systematic error
reference: Anderson J. D., Lau E. L., Giampieri G. 2003, arXiv:gr-qc/0308010v1 (withdrawn 24 Oct 2003)
notes: v2 (24 Oct 2003): 'This paper was withdrawn at the recommendation of the Cassini Radio Science Team.' Not a published result; superseded by the 2004 proceedings.

data_used: closed-loop Doppler (Block V, the kind of data in PDS ODFs): 1697 points after plasma calibration, 1575 in 17 passes after troposphere (AWVR) calibration; first pass after conjunction deleted
method: ODP batch-sequential fit, 4 batches; 8 parameters: 6 state (epoch 6 June 2002 20:42:04.1848 ET) + constant acceleration ATAR toward Earth (stochastic per batch) + gamma
quote: In terms of the standard post-Newtonian parameter γ, we find that γ − 1 = (−1.3 ± 5.2) × 10⁻⁵, in agreement with the theory of General Relativity.
reference: Anderson J. D., Lau E. L., Giampieri G. 2004, Proc. 22nd Texas Symp. Relativistic Astrophysics, eConf C041213, paper 0305
notes: Table I: ATAR = -61.38 +- 1.57 (1e-13 km/s^2), chi2/(N-8) = 0.966, N = 1575; residual sigma 3.95 (pre) and 3.98 (post) micron/s. Plasma combination y = 1.0575901 y_Ka - 0.0575901 y_X. 'data within one day of conjunction are useless, even with the Ka-Band uplink'. Residuals 'would be symmetric about conjunction if the Ka transmitter at DSS25 had not failed for four scheduled passes just prior to conjunction'.
